sm: The episode opens with a montage from the film Confession, set in a Soviet prison, in which a man is arrested under Article 58 for counter-revolutionary activity and is told that everyone breaks. Clips of recent news headlines about tariffs, a government shutdown and immigration enforcement are cut in. Then the cast and crew talk about the project. One actor says Ben Shapiro texted him out of the blue asking whether he knew a leading man in his fifties for a script he had written. He read it and was blown away, and he says this kind of material rarely gets written or made. He also talks about working with Rob Lowe, an old friend, and says his character interrogates his former professor.

Actors describe making the film. One says it was the most exacting and focused experience of his career, with an emotionally major scene every single day and no rest, like going from a sauna to a cold plunge. Emile Hirsch, Jennifer Jason Leigh, Cody Smit-McPhee and Richard Brake introduce their characters, a prisoner, Anya, Sasha and Bogdan. They say every character in the script is complex, and that the film is a debate about faith and atheism that leaves viewers to decide what they believe. They prepared by watching documentaries about the Gulag and reading the book Whispers. One actor jokes that he prepared a Russian accent and then learned that nobody would speak Russian. The part ends with the first day on set and the director's way of working.

Cast members recall the director setting the camera on a pyramid in the middle of the cell and slowly turning it around. They say fourteen-page scenes were broken into small moments and shot on film. They praise Rob Lowe and Nick Nolte, and say they hope viewers will dwell on the idea of faith. The crew then describes the sets. The building that inspired them was built in 1888 as a hotel and later taken over by the KGB, with cells and execution rooms below street level. The production designer built the sets in about two to two and a half weeks using recycled walls. The aim was an environment that felt aggressive and cold, with humidity and running water on the walls, and one actor instinctively moved his head away from a wall.

The director is praised as having an extraordinary visual gift. The film takes place in about five rooms and a few hallways, shot on thirty-five millimeter negative in an anamorphic ratio. On set there was no shot list and no rehearsal, only about fifteen minutes of talk about motivation, and he creates each shot in the moment. Ben Shapiro says the first time he heard actors say his words was on set, which was both terrifying and rewarding. Shapiro says he wants to show that conservative filmmakers can make great movies without the quota systems and awards politics of the industry. Viewers then react, mostly with strong praise for the cast and for James Franco as the Soviet villain, though one says he disliked it.

More reactions follow. Viewers call the film beautiful, claustrophobic and carried by its dialogue, and one calls it one of the most Christian movies he has seen. The hosts then begin their discussion. One host says conservatives rarely produce good art, and admits he was moved and proud of Ben. Ben Shapiro says it is a major step forward for the company, noting that the director was nominated for the Venice Golden Lion and that the cast has seven Oscar nominations among them. He calls it the first project that is film first while deeply rooted in Christianity and anti-communism. Another host says a film makes you feel an argument rather than just hear it, and he praises the performances and the emotional landing.

The hosts keep praising the film, and one says it felt like a breakthrough after conservative films that were like faith-based films he could not stand. Shapiro explains the casting. A well-known actor first signed on for the professor role but was conflicted out. Rob Lowe then asked to read the script, called back in tears, and begged to play the broken, alcoholic professor, offering to shave his head. Franco and the director joined next, and Brad Dourif was cast on short notice after another actor died during filming. Shapiro praises Richard Brake as a terrifying committed Marxist and says the film is built around characters rather than arguments. He notes the shooting script was only eighty-two pages and the film plays like a stage play.

Shapiro explains he started from constraints, writing a film set almost entirely in two rooms. He calls Rob Lowe the quiet center, which lets Franco and Brake go bigger. He cites his influences, including Timothy Snyder's Bloodlands for the famine story, Arthur Koestler's Darkness at Noon, and references to Vasily Grossman, Pushkin and Chekhov, with the end built on Dostoevsky's Grand Inquisitor. A host says conservative and faith films often fear giving the hero a real flaw, while this one opens with the hero licking vodka off the floor, which makes his redemption land harder. They hope the film is a gateway to reading, and joke that Dostoevsky is right about everything while Tolstoy observes human nature better.

Asked why now, Shapiro says he was not consciously responding to politics. He had been reading a lot of history and kept spotting echoes of earlier eras. The company's board approved the script, and his elevator pitch was that it is the most anti-communist, pro-Christian film ever made. A host says the core problem with communism is that it hates God, not just that its economics fail, and that Christianity costs something. Shapiro discusses the final confrontation, in which the hero confesses both a crime against the state and his faith. He says he had thought of the hero as the good guy, and that redemption requires repentance and sacrifice. He notes the hero does not go home happy, and that the story shows saints often start badly.

The hosts discuss the ending, in which the hero confesses, kisses Franco's character on the forehead as a signal, and Franco then goes home and reads the end of the Grand Inquisitor. They mention the theme of adoption through the student. Shapiro says the director shot on thirty-five millimeter film in two-minute segments rather than full scenes, which demanded sustained intensity from the actors. They praise the moving camera, which keeps the dungeon rooms from feeling static, and note the film has no score apart from music at the start and end. They compare this with No Country for Old Men and say it works here. A host says he had to stand up during the opening scene in the tiny standing cell, which the director added to the script.

Shapiro says the director grew up in Eastern Europe under communism, and so he suggested adding the standing cell, which was a real Soviet practice. The director also added cutaway shots of Franco reacting while Lowe speaks to his son, and the actors added touches such as swirling the vodka glass. In another case the director wanted Franco to tell Lowe to kneel, and Shapiro suggested he ask politely, saying kneel please, which is more frightening. The hosts talk about how actors give the words humanity. Shapiro says the story is grounded in real history and that some details, like how prisoners are moved in the Lubyanka, were altered for drama. The whole set was built from scratch on a sound stage in Los Angeles from historical photographs.

A host says conservatives prefer the literal and practical, and asks whether it is an overstatement that political opponents would put them against the wall. The hosts say some would be happy to, pointing to the celebration of Charlie Kirk's death. They then watch a streamer's reaction to the film's trailer, in which he is baffled that Rob Lowe and James Franco star in a Shapiro screenplay. The hosts mock him and say the outrage shows the left feels threatened that conservatives are playing in their sandbox. Shapiro says the company wants the best people at what they do, not only conservatives, and names a casting rule of whether a Louisiana cousin would recognize the face.

The hosts read praise from Glenn Beck, David Limbaugh and Rod Dreher, who called the film one of the most philosophically and theologically profound he has seen. Shapiro says a rumor circulated that he had been seen at brunch with someone else, but he was actually having brunch with Rob Lowe in Los Angeles. The hosts joke about a ten thousand dollar reward and about funding a book. Shapiro says the angry reaction to Confession was greater than the reaction to the more provocative Infidels, because a film with artistic credibility disrupts the culture in a way trolling does not. The hosts call it a relevant, historically grounded and spiritually edifying movie about what faith in Christ costs, and sign off.
